title: Spending on family
tomorrow: Jordan's grandma gives at church. what's Dadi's version?

lines: A RECEIPT AS LONG AS AN ARM.
cards: A grocery receipt as long as an arm. Rent on the first. A kid who needs new shoes, again.
A phone bill for a parent who doesn't know how to switch plans. None of it looks like giving. It looks like bills.
A short line in Sahih al-Bukhari says otherwise. The Prophet ﷺ said: when a man spends on his family, seeking reward, it is counted for him as charity.

teach.b: Two words in that line do the work: seeking reward. The groceries are the same groceries. What changes them is the intention, the same thing that turned a shift into worship last week.
Another hadith, in Sahih Muslim, puts four coins side by side: a dinar spent in God's path, a dinar to free a slave, a dinar given to a poor person, and a dinar spent on your family.
The greatest in reward, the Prophet said, is the one spent on your family. That surprises people who think charity has to go out the door.

The companion Sa'd, sick and thinking of giving away nearly everything, was told something similar: leave your heirs well off, and know that whatever you spend for God's sake is rewarded, even the bite of food you lift to your wife's mouth.

And the Qur'an, asked what people should spend, begins its answer with parents and near relatives before it names orphans, the needy and the traveler. So the circle widens outward from home, and home is already inside it.
One to tell a friend: in that hadith, the coin spent on your own family outweighs the other three.

how: Muslims provide for their households as a duty and, with a good intention, count it as charity; many begin their giving with parents and close relatives before widening it out.

o: a yearly gift to relatives at the Eid feast
providing for your household, counted as charity
giving savings away so the family won't inherit

games.q: the coins and the circle — tap the pairs.
p: greatest of the four in reward

s: in a hadith, the coin spent on your family has the greatest reward of four
Muslim 995: in God's path, to free a slave, to the poor, on your family. the family dinar is greatest.
in Islam, charity only counts when it goes to strangers
spending on family, seeking reward, is counted as charity.
the intention behind paying household bills makes no difference
the hadith says 'seeking reward': the same groceries, meant for God, become charity.

games.q: your cousin sends money home to his parents each month and feels guilty he has nothing left for the masjid's fundraiser. what fits?
o: he's falling short; real charity is the fundraiser, not family.
what he sends home, meant for God, is already charity.
he should split every paycheck evenly between parents and masjid.
games.why: spending on family, seeking reward, is counted as charity, and in Muslim's report the family dinar is the greatest in reward.

practice: Count on your fingers the people whose food, rent or care passes through your hands, or whose care passes to you. One name per finger, and one thing that went between you this week. Let the count end in thanks.

wordCard.voice: Spending on family: providing for the people at home, with God in mind, and counted as charity. Even the grocery bag.

orig.note: Arabic: spending, especially what one spends to provide for one's family.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: family is charity, when it's meant for God. Home is inside the circle.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 55 (a man's spending on his family, seeking reward, is charity for him)
Sahih al-Bukhari 56 (to Sa'd: whatever you spend for God's sake is rewarded, even the morsel you put in your wife's mouth); see also Bukhari 2742 on leaving heirs well off
Sahih Muslim 995 (four dinars; the one spent on your family is greatest in reward)
Qur'an 2:215 (what to spend: on parents and near kindred, orphans, the needy and the wayfarer)
